subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Computer Laboratory Rules, Safety and Basic Maintenance
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - THEORY
TOPIC: Rules and Requirements of the Computer Laboratory; Basic Maintenance of Computers

1. WHY THE COMPUTER LABORATORY HAS SPECIAL RULES
A computer laboratory (computer room) is a special classroom set aside for learning and practising
computer skills. It contains delicate and expensive electronic equipment - computers, monitors,
keyboards, printers, and sometimes a server and networking cables - that can easily be damaged by
dust, liquids, careless handling, power problems or overcrowding. Because the equipment is shared by
many classes and is costly to replace or repair (especially in a country like Zimbabwe where importing
computer parts can be expensive and slow), every pupil must follow agreed rules so that the laboratory
stays safe, clean and usable for everyone.

2. BASIC RULES OF THE COMPUTER LABORATORY
Pupils should be able to state and explain rules such as:
   a) No eating or drinking in the computer laboratory - food crumbs and spilt liquids (tea, water,
      juice) can fall into the keyboard or vents of the system unit and cause short-circuits or sticky,
      jammed keys.
   b) No running, pushing or playing rough games in the laboratory - computers, monitors and desks can
      be knocked over, and pupils can be hurt by trailing cables.
   c) Wash and dry hands before touching the keyboard and mouse - dirty or wet hands transfer dirt and
      moisture onto the equipment and can cause rusting of metal parts.
   d) Do not insert foreign objects (pins, coins, sticks) into any socket, disk drive or USB port.
   e) Sit properly on the chair, keep bags and coats away from walkways so no one trips over them.
   f) Switch on and switch off equipment only in the correct sequence and only with permission/guidance
      from the teacher.
   g) Report any fault (a computer not switching on, a cracked screen, a loose cable) to the teacher
      immediately instead of trying to fix it yourself.
   h) Do not bring magnets, or strong magnetic toys, near computers, because magnetic fields can damage
      data stored on some types of storage media.
   i) Leave the laboratory clean and tidy - push in chairs, switch off machines properly, and do not
      litter.
   j) Never insert an unknown flash disk/memory stick from home into a school computer without the
      teacher's permission - it may carry a computer virus.

Pupils are usually asked, as a class activity, to help formulate (write, in their own words) a class
set of computer laboratory rules and to discuss the consequences of breaking them (for example, a
pupil who runs and knocks over a monitor could injure a classmate and destroy expensive equipment that
the whole school then goes without).

3. ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS FOR A COMPUTER LABORATORY
Computers are sensitive machines and work best, and last longer, under the right environmental
conditions:
   - Ventilation: There should be enough fresh air movement (through windows, fans, or air
     conditioning) because computers generate heat when running, and overheating can damage internal
     components. A stuffy, closed room causes machines to overheat and can shorten their working life.
   - Temperature: The room should not be too hot or too cold. Direct, strong sunlight falling onto
     screens or system units should be avoided (curtains/blinds help).
   - Dust control: Dust settles inside the system unit and on circuit boards, causing components to
     overheat or malfunction. Floors should be kept clean, and dust covers can be used on machines that
     are not in use.
   - Humidity: Very damp conditions can cause rusting and short-circuits, while very dry conditions can
     build up static electricity, which can damage sensitive electronic chips.
   - Lighting: The room should be well lit, but light should not cause glare/reflection on the screen,
     as this strains the eyes.

4. SECURITY OF AND IN THE COMPUTER LABORATORY
   - Doors and windows should be fitted with strong locks/burglar bars, since computers are valuable
     and can be stolen.
   - Windows may need grilles, and the room should have a working fire extinguisher.
   - A register/sign-in system may be used so the teacher knows which pupils used which machine and
     when, which helps if a fault is later discovered.
   - Cables should be neatly arranged (trunked along walls or floors) so that they are not a tripping
     hazard and cannot easily be pulled loose.
   - Only authorised persons should be allowed to move or repair equipment.

5. POWER-RELATED CONSIDERATIONS (Important in the Zimbabwean context)
Because power supply in many parts of Zimbabwe can be unreliable (load-shedding, voltage surges when
power returns), computer laboratories are encouraged to use:
   - Surge protectors / surge protector blocks - these guard the computer against sudden voltage spikes
     that can permanently damage the system unit when electricity is restored after a power cut.
   - An Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS), where available, which keeps the computer running for a
     short time after a power cut so work can be saved safely and the machine shut down properly instead
     of switching off abruptly.
   - Correct shutdown procedures - never simply switching off the wall socket or pulling the plug while
     a computer is running, because this can corrupt (damage) files that were open and can shorten the
     life of the hard disk.

6. BASIC MAINTENANCE OF COMPUTERS (Grade 7 focus)
"Maintenance" means looking after equipment so that it continues to work well and lasts a long time.
At Grade 7 level, maintenance is kept simple and practical:
   a) Keeping computers free of dust - wiping the outside of the monitor and system unit with a soft,
      dry cloth; not using a wet cloth on electronic parts; keeping the floor swept so dust is not
      stirred up into the air.
   b) Using dust covers on machines when the laboratory is not in use, especially overnight or during
      school holidays.
   c) Using surge protectors/protector blocks to protect computers from power surges.
   d) Not blocking the air vents on the system unit or monitor, since blocked vents cause overheating.
   e) Keeping food, drinks and liquids completely away from all equipment.
   f) Handling the mouse, keyboard and other parts gently - not banging keys, not dragging the mouse by
      its cable, not slamming the lid of a laptop.
   g) Reporting problems early rather than waiting for equipment to fail completely, and having
      equipment serviced (professionally checked and cleaned/repaired) periodically by a qualified
      technician.
   h) Keeping cables tidy and untangled to prevent them from being damaged or becoming a safety hazard.
NOTE: At Grade 7, "maintenance" is understood at the level of explaining WHY cleaning and servicing
matter - pupils are not expected to open up or repair a computer themselves.

KEY TERMS
   - Computer laboratory: a special room equipped with computers for teaching and learning ICT skills.
   - Ventilation: the movement of fresh air into and out of a room.
   - Surge protector: a device that protects electronic equipment from sudden increases in electrical
     voltage.
   - Maintenance: the routine care and upkeep of equipment to keep it working properly.
   - Dust cover: a cloth or plastic cover placed over equipment to protect it from dust when not in
     use.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. State four rules that should be followed in a computer laboratory.
   2. Explain why good ventilation is important in a computer laboratory.
   3. Why should pupils avoid eating or drinking near computers?
   4. Name one device that protects a computer from power surges, and explain how it helps.
   5. Give two examples of basic computer maintenance a Grade 7 pupil can help with.
   6. Explain two dangers of switching off a computer at the wall socket without shutting it down
      properly first.
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Types of Computers
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - THEORY
TOPIC: Different Types of Computers

1. WHAT IS A COMPUTER?
A computer is an electronic device that accepts data (raw facts and figures) as input, processes that
data by following a set of instructions (a program), stores data, and produces information as output.
Computers are used at home, in schools, in banks, in hospitals, in shops, in government offices and in
industry because they can work quickly, accurately and can store huge amounts of information.

2. TYPES OF COMPUTERS BY SIZE, PURPOSE AND PORTABILITY
At Grade 7, pupils must be able to identify and compare the following types of computers:

   a) DESKTOP COMPUTER / PERSONAL COMPUTER (PC)
      A computer designed to stay in one place on a desk or table. It usually has a separate system
      unit (the box holding the main processing parts), a monitor, keyboard and mouse connected by
      cables. Desktops are commonly found in offices, schools and homes because they are affordable,
      powerful for their price, and easy to repair or upgrade part by part.

   b) LAPTOP COMPUTER
      A portable, folding computer that combines the system unit, screen, keyboard and a built-in
      pointing device (touchpad) into one case. It runs on a rechargeable battery as well as mains
      electricity, so it can be carried around and used in places without a fixed power supply -
      useful in Zimbabwe where power cuts are common, since a fully charged laptop can keep working
      during load-shedding.

   c) NOTEBOOK COMPUTER
      A smaller and lighter version of a laptop, designed mainly for portability and basic tasks such
      as word processing, browsing and communication, rather than heavy processing work.

   d) PALMTOP COMPUTER / PDA (Personal Digital Assistant)
      A very small computer that can fit in the palm of a hand or a pocket. Palmtops have limited
      processing power compared to laptops or desktops and are mainly used for simple tasks like
      keeping contacts, notes, a calendar/diary, or small calculations. Many features of old-style
      palmtops are now found inside modern smartphones.

   e) MAINFRAME COMPUTER
      A very large, powerful and expensive computer used by big organisations (for example large
      banks, insurance companies, government departments or big companies with branches countrywide)
      to process huge volumes of data and to allow many users (sometimes thousands) to work on the
      system through terminals at the same time. Mainframes are known for being extremely reliable and
      able to run without stopping for long periods.

   f) SUPERCOMPUTER
      The most powerful category of computer, built to perform extremely complex and fast calculations
      - for example weather forecasting and climate modelling, scientific research, space exploration
      calculations, and simulations. Supercomputers are very expensive and are usually found only in
      major research institutions, government scientific agencies or large universities, not in
      ordinary schools or offices.

3. COMPARING THE TYPES OF COMPUTERS
   - Size: Supercomputers and mainframes are the largest and often fill a whole room; desktops are
     medium sized; laptops and notebooks are smaller and foldable; palmtops are the smallest, fitting
     in a hand.
   - Portability: Palmtops are the most portable, followed by notebooks, then laptops. Desktops,
     mainframes and supercomputers are not portable - they stay fixed in one location.
   - Cost: Supercomputers and mainframes are the most expensive; desktops are relatively affordable;
     laptops, notebooks and palmtops vary depending on their features.
   - Processing power: Supercomputers have the greatest processing power, followed by mainframes.
     Desktops and laptops have moderate power suited to everyday tasks. Palmtops have the least
     processing power of the group.
   - Number of users: A mainframe or supercomputer can serve many users working at the same time on
     linked terminals; a desktop, laptop, notebook or palmtop is normally used by one person at a time.

4. WHERE EACH TYPE IS COMMONLY USED (EXAMPLES RELEVANT TO ZIMBABWE)
   - A rural or urban school computer laboratory: mostly desktop computers, sometimes with a few
     laptops donated by NGOs or bought by the school.
   - A bank such as one on a Zimbabwean high street: mainframe computers to process thousands of
     customer transactions safely and quickly, with staff using desktop terminals connected to the
     mainframe.
   - A travelling businessperson or a teacher preparing lessons at home and at school: a laptop or
     notebook for portability.
   - A person keeping a small personal diary and contact list on the move: a palmtop or, more commonly
     today, a smartphone that has taken over many of the palmtop's original functions.
   - A university or research centre doing weather prediction for the Southern African region:
     supercomputers.

KEY TERMS
   - Computer: an electronic device that accepts, processes, stores and outputs data as information.
   - Portability: how easily a device can be carried from place to place.
   - Terminal: a device (screen and keyboard) used to access a larger, central computer such as a
     mainframe.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Name any four types of computers.
   2. State one difference between a laptop and a desktop computer.
   3. Give one example of an organisation that would use a mainframe computer, and explain why.
   4. Which type of computer would a supercomputer be used for, and why?
   5. Explain why a laptop can be useful during a power cut, while a desktop cannot be used at all
      during that time.
   6. Arrange the following from the smallest to the largest in physical size: mainframe, palmtop,
      laptop, desktop.
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Computer Hardware: Input, Output and Storage Devices
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - THEORY
TOPIC: Computer Hardware - Input, Output and Storage Devices

1. WHAT IS HARDWARE?
Hardware refers to all the physical, touchable parts of a computer system - the parts you can see and
hold, as opposed to software, which is the set of invisible instructions/programs that tell the
hardware what to do. Hardware is generally grouped into: input devices, output devices, the system
unit (processing), and storage devices.

2. THE SYSTEM UNIT
The system unit is the main box/casing of a desktop computer (or the main body of a laptop) that
houses the central processing unit (CPU) - often called the "brain" of the computer - along with the
motherboard, memory (RAM), the internal hard disk, and connection ports for other devices. All
processing of data into information happens inside the system unit.

3. INPUT DEVICES
Input devices are hardware used to enter data and instructions INTO the computer.
   - Keyboard: a set of keys (letters, numbers, symbols and special/function keys) used to type text,
     numbers and commands into the computer.
   - Mouse: a small hand-held pointing device used to move the on-screen pointer, select items, open
     programs, and give commands by clicking and dragging.
   - Other input devices pupils should be able to recognise: a scanner (converts a paper document or
     picture into a digital image the computer can store), a microphone (inputs sound), and a webcam
     (inputs pictures/video).

4. OUTPUT DEVICES
Output devices are hardware used to present processed data (information) FROM the computer to the
user, usually in a form people can see, hear, or hold as a printed copy.
   - Screen/Monitor: displays text, pictures and video so the user can see what the computer is doing;
     this is called "soft copy" output because nothing is printed on paper.
   - Printer: produces a paper copy (called "hard copy") of documents, letters, pictures or reports.
   - Speakers: output sound, such as music, spoken instructions, or the audio of a video.
Pupils are expected to be able to classify a given list of devices correctly into "input" or "output",
for example: keyboard (input), mouse (input), monitor (output), printer (output), speakers (output),
scanner (input).

5. STORAGE DEVICES
Storage devices are used to save data and programs so that they are not lost when the computer is
switched off, and so that files can be moved between computers or kept safely for future use.
   - Hard disk (internal storage): a storage device fixed inside the system unit that stores the
     computer's operating system, installed programs, and the user's files. It has a large storage
     capacity compared to portable storage media.
   - Floppy disk: an older, small, thin magnetic disk in a plastic case, once commonly used to store
     and transfer small amounts of data. It is largely outdated today because it stores very little
     data and is easily damaged, but Grade 7 pupils should still be able to identify it, since it
     appears in the official syllabus as historical/background knowledge.
   - Flash disk / memory stick (USB flash drive): a small, portable storage device that plugs into a
     USB port. It is popular because it is small, durable, holds a relatively large amount of data, and
     is reusable (data can be written, deleted and rewritten many times).
   - Compact Disk (CD): a flat, round, plastic disk that stores data optically (read by a laser) and is
     commonly used to store music, software or documents.
   - Digital Video Disk (DVD): similar to a CD but able to store much more data, commonly used for
     storing videos/movies as well as large files or software.

6. COMPARING STORAGE DEVICES
   - Storage capacity (how much data fits): generally, hard disks store the most, followed by DVDs,
     then CDs, then flash disks (though modern flash disks can now hold more than older CDs/DVDs), and
     floppy disks store the least.
   - Portability: flash disks, CDs, DVDs and floppy disks can be carried around and used on different
     computers; a hard disk usually stays fixed inside one system unit (unless it is an external hard
     disk).
   - Durability: flash disks tend to be more resistant to knocks than CDs/DVDs, which can be scratched,
     and more reliable than floppy disks, which are easily damaged by dust, heat and magnets.

7. IDENTIFYING AND LABELLING HARDWARE (Practical Skill)
Pupils practise this topic by drawing and labelling the parts of a computer they see in their own
laboratory, and by physically pointing to and naming: the system unit, the keyboard, the mouse, the
monitor/screen, the speakers, and the printer, and by sorting a list of devices/storage media into the
correct category (input, output, or storage). Teachers restrict examples to equipment that is actually
available in the school's own computer laboratory wherever possible.

KEY TERMS
   - Hardware: the physical parts of a computer that can be seen and touched.
   - Input device: hardware used to enter data into a computer.
   - Output device: hardware used to present processed information to the user.
   - Storage device: hardware/media used to save data for later use.
   - Hard copy: printed output on paper.
   - Soft copy: output displayed on a screen, not printed.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Define the term "hardware".
   2. Classify the following as INPUT or OUTPUT devices: mouse, printer, keyboard, monitor, speakers.
   3. Name three examples of storage devices.
   4. State one advantage of a flash disk over a floppy disk.
   5. Explain the difference between a hard copy and a soft copy, giving one example of each.
   6. What is stored inside the system unit that allows the computer to process data?
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Computer Software: System and Application Software
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - THEORY
TOPIC: Computer Software - System and Application Software

1. WHAT IS SOFTWARE?
Software is the set of instructions, programs and related data that tell computer hardware what to do
and how to do it. Unlike hardware, software cannot be touched - it is intangible - but it can be seen
running on the screen and stored on a storage device. Without software, hardware alone cannot perform
any useful task; the two work together.

2. SYSTEM SOFTWARE
System software manages and controls the computer's own hardware and resources so that other programs
can run properly. The most important example pupils must know is the Operating System (OS).
   - Operating System (OS): the main system software that starts up when the computer is switched on,
     manages the computer's memory, files, and hardware devices, and provides the user interface (icons,
     windows, the desktop, the start menu) that a person uses to interact with the computer. Examples
     that pupils may encounter include Windows, which is widely used in Zimbabwean school computer
     laboratories.
   - Without an operating system, a computer cannot load or run any other program, because the
     operating system is what allows the hardware and other software to "talk" to each other.

3. APPLICATION SOFTWARE
Application software (often just called "applications" or "apps" or "programs") is software designed
to help the user perform specific tasks, rather than to manage the computer itself. Examples that
Grade 7 pupils use directly in this syllabus include:
   - A word processing program - used to type, edit and format text documents such as letters,
     compositions and stories.
   - A spreadsheet program - used to organise numbers and data in rows and columns, perform
     calculations, and create charts/graphs.
   - A presentation program - used to create slide shows for presenting information, often including
     text, pictures and animation effects.
   - A drawing/paint program - used to create and colour pictures and shapes.
   - An internet browser - used to open and view websites on the internet.
   - An e-mail program - used to send and receive electronic mail.
   - Anti-virus software - a special type of application software used to detect, block and remove
     computer viruses to keep the computer safe.

4. TELLING SYSTEM SOFTWARE AND APPLICATION SOFTWARE APART
   - System software works mainly for the COMPUTER (managing hardware, memory and files) and normally
     starts running automatically when the computer is switched on.
   - Application software works mainly for the USER, helping them complete a specific job such as
     typing a letter, calculating a budget, or drawing a picture, and it must usually be opened
     deliberately by the user (for example by clicking its icon).
   - A simple way to remember it: the operating system is like the manager of a school who keeps
     everything running smoothly in the background, while application software is like a teacher doing
     a specific job (teaching Mathematics, or teaching English) that the school was set up for in the
     first place.

5. IDENTIFYING SOFTWARE IN USE (Practical Skill)
Pupils practise identifying which program is currently open/in use on a school computer by looking at
the title bar at the top of the window, the icon shown on the task bar, or the icon on the desktop, and
naming the software and stating its general purpose (for example, "this is a word processing program,
used for typing documents").

KEY TERMS
   - Software: the instructions/programs that tell computer hardware what to do.
   - Operating system: system software that manages the computer's hardware, memory and files, and
     provides the interface the user works with.
   - Application software: programs designed to help a user perform a specific task.
   - Anti-virus software: application software used to detect and remove computer viruses.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Define the term "software" and explain how it differs from hardware.
   2. What is the main purpose of an operating system?
   3. Give three examples of application software and state what each one is used for.
   4. Classify the following as SYSTEM software or APPLICATION software: Windows operating system,
      a word processor, anti-virus software, a presentation program.
   5. Explain, in your own words, why a computer cannot run a word processing program without an
      operating system already running.
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Computer Viruses: Causes, Effects and Protection
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - THEORY
TOPIC: Computer Viruses and Their Effects

1. WHAT IS A COMPUTER VIRUS?
A computer virus is a harmful computer program written on purpose to spread from one computer or
storage device to another, and to interfere with the normal working of a computer, often without the
user's knowledge or permission. It is called a "virus" because, like a biological virus that spreads
between people and makes them sick, a computer virus copies itself and spreads between machines,
"infecting" them and often causing harm.

2. HOW COMPUTER VIRUSES SPREAD (CAUSES)
Grade 7 pupils should be able to identify common ways viruses spread, which is very relevant given how
widely flash disks are shared between school computers in Zimbabwe:
   - Using an infected flash disk/memory stick on a clean computer, or a clean flash disk on an
     infected computer - the virus copies itself onto the new storage device or computer.
   - Downloading files, programs or attachments from the internet or from e-mail messages without
     checking them first.
   - Opening e-mail attachments from unknown or suspicious senders.
   - Copying files from an already infected computer or storage device (CD, DVD, external hard disk)
     without scanning them first.
   - Installing pirated or unofficial copies of software from untrustworthy sources.
   - Connecting to unprotected/unsafe networks.

3. EFFECTS (SIGNS/DAMAGE CAUSED BY) A COMPUTER VIRUS
   - Files can be deleted, corrupted (damaged so they will not open properly), or hidden without the
     user's permission.
   - The computer may run much more slowly than usual, or may freeze/hang frequently.
   - Some programs may refuse to open, or may crash unexpectedly.
   - Strange pop-up messages, unusual icons, or unfamiliar programs may appear.
   - Some viruses can steal private information, or allow an outsider to control the computer without
     permission.
   - In serious cases, a virus can make the whole computer stop working properly, requiring a
     technician to clean or reinstall the operating system.
   - Viruses can spread further, silently infecting every flash disk plugged into the machine,
     spreading the damage to other computers, including at home or at school.

4. PROTECTING A COMPUTER FROM VIRUSES
   - Install and regularly update anti-virus software, which scans the computer, detects known
     viruses, and removes or quarantines (isolates) them.
   - Scan any flash disk, CD, DVD or external hard disk with anti-virus software BEFORE opening any
     files stored on it, especially before use on a school computer that many different pupils share.
   - Avoid opening e-mail attachments or links from senders you do not know or do not trust.
   - Avoid downloading software, games or files from unofficial or suspicious websites.
   - Do not use pirated software, since it is a common source of hidden viruses.
   - Keep the operating system and application software updated, since updates often close security
     weaknesses that viruses use to spread.
   - Back up (make a safety copy of) important files regularly onto a separate storage device, so that
     if a virus does destroy data, a safe copy still exists elsewhere.
   - Report a suspected virus infection to the teacher/technician immediately rather than continuing to
     use the affected machine or plugging more flash disks into it.

5. DISCUSSION: WHY THIS MATTERS IN A SCHOOL COMPUTER LABORATORY
Because many different pupils plug their own personal flash disks into the same shared school
computers to save schoolwork, a school computer laboratory is a common place for viruses to spread very
quickly from one flash disk to many others in a single day. This is why the syllabus expects pupils to
understand not just what a virus is, but practical habits (like scanning storage devices with anti-
virus software before opening files) that stop the spread.

KEY TERMS
   - Computer virus: a harmful program that copies itself and spreads between computers/storage
     devices, interfering with normal operation.
   - Anti-virus software: a program that detects, blocks and removes viruses.
   - Corrupted file: a file that has been damaged so that it can no longer be opened or used normally.
   - Backup: a safety copy of data kept in case the original is lost or damaged.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Define a computer virus.
   2. State three ways in which a computer virus can spread from one computer to another.
   3. Describe three signs that show a computer may be infected with a virus.
   4. Explain two ways of protecting a computer from viruses.
   5. Why is it especially important to scan a flash disk with anti-virus software before using it on a
      shared school computer?
   6. What should a pupil do if they suspect the computer they are using has a virus?
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Advantages and Disadvantages of Using Computers; Benefits and Limitations of the Internet and E-mail
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - THEORY
TOPIC: Advantages and Disadvantages of Using Computers; Benefits and Limitations of the Internet and
E-mail

1. ADVANTAGES OF USING COMPUTERS
   - Speed: computers process large amounts of data and perform calculations far faster than a human
     could by hand.
   - Accuracy: computers do not get tired or careless, so they reduce mistakes that can happen with
     manual (by-hand) work, as long as correct data and instructions are given.
   - Storage: computers can store enormous amounts of information in a small physical space (for
     example, thousands of documents on one flash disk), compared to paper files that take up large
     amounts of cupboard/shelf space.
   - Communication: computers connected to the internet allow people to communicate instantly across
     long distances through e-mail, video calls and messaging, which is useful for a country like
     Zimbabwe where family members and business partners are often spread across different towns,
     provinces or even countries.
   - Automation and efficiency: repetitive tasks (like calculating totals in a spreadsheet, or printing
     many copies of a letter) can be done quickly and repeated exactly the same way every time.
   - Access to information: the internet gives access to a huge range of information for research,
     schoolwork, news and learning that would otherwise be very hard to find locally.
   - Entertainment and creativity: computers support music, games, drawing, videos and design work.

2. DISADVANTAGES OF USING COMPUTERS
   - Cost: computers, software, maintenance and internet access can be expensive to buy and to keep
     running, which can make them hard to afford for some families and schools.
   - Health issues: sitting for long periods can cause poor posture, eye strain from staring at a
     screen too long, or wrist strain from typing, if good habits are not followed.
   - Dependence on electricity: computers cannot work without power, so they are affected by power cuts
     - a real challenge in areas of Zimbabwe that experience load-shedding.
   - Risk of viruses and data loss: as covered in the previous topic, computers can be infected by
     viruses, and data can be lost through hardware failure, accidental deletion, or theft of the
     device.
   - Job changes: some tasks that used to be done by many people by hand can now be done faster by
     fewer people using computers, which can change the types of jobs available in society.
   - Reduced physical activity/social interaction: too much time spent on a computer or phone can
     reduce time spent on physical exercise or face-to-face interaction with family and friends.
   - Exposure to inappropriate or false content: without supervision, internet users (including
     children) may come across content that is unsuitable, or information that is simply incorrect.

3. BENEFITS OF USING THE INTERNET AND E-MAIL
   - Instant communication: e-mail allows written messages, and often attached files, to be sent and
     received within seconds, anywhere there is an internet connection, which is far quicker and often
     cheaper than sending a letter by post.
   - Research and learning: the internet gives access to encyclopaedias, educational websites, videos
     and news from all over the world, supporting schoolwork and lifelong learning.
   - Sharing documents and files: e-mail attachments and cloud storage make it possible to send
     photographs, documents, and other files to someone far away almost instantly.
   - Access to services: many services (banking, applying for documents, buying goods, checking exam
     results) can increasingly be accessed online, saving the time and cost of travelling in person.
   - Keeping in touch with family: many Zimbabwean families have relatives working or studying in other
     towns or other countries, and e-mail, together with other internet-based communication, helps them
     to stay in touch regularly and cheaply.

4. LIMITATIONS OF THE INTERNET AND E-MAIL
   - Cost of data/connectivity: internet access requires a data bundle, Wi-Fi subscription, or airtime,
     which is a real, ongoing cost, and connectivity is not equally available or affordable everywhere,
     especially in some rural areas.
   - Security risks: e-mail can be used to spread viruses through attachments, and can be used for
     "spam" (unwanted junk messages) or by dishonest people to try to trick users into giving away
     personal information (this is called phishing).
   - Unreliable networks: internet connections can be slow or can fail, especially during power cuts or
     in areas with poor network coverage.
   - Misinformation: not everything found on the internet is true or accurate, so information found
     there should always be checked against a trusted source before it is fully believed or used.
   - Privacy concerns: personal information shared online can sometimes be accessed or misused by
     people it was not intended for, if proper security precautions (like strong passwords) are not
     used.

5. BALANCED THINKING (Class Discussion Skill)
The syllabus expects pupils to be able to DISCUSS both sides sensibly - for example, weighing the
benefit of fast communication by e-mail against the risk of viruses spreading through e-mail
attachments, and suggesting how the risk can be reduced (for example, by not opening attachments from
unknown senders and using anti-virus software), rather than only listing points without understanding
them.

KEY TERMS
   - Advantage: a benefit or positive point of using something.
   - Disadvantage/limitation: a drawback or negative point of using something.
   - Spam: unwanted junk e-mail messages, often sent in bulk.
   - Phishing: a dishonest attempt, often by e-mail, to trick someone into giving away private
     information such as passwords.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. State three advantages of using computers.
   2. State three disadvantages of using computers.
   3. Explain two benefits of using e-mail to communicate with family who live far away.
   4. Explain two limitations of using the internet in Zimbabwe.
   5. "Computers bring both benefits and problems to society." Discuss this statement using at least
      two points on each side.
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Starting Up, Shutting Down and Using the Mouse (Right-Clicking)
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - BASIC SETTINGS AND FILE MANAGEMENT
TOPIC: Starting Up and Shutting Down the Computer; Use of the Mouse (Right-Clicking)

1. STARTING UP A COMPUTER
Starting up (also called "booting") a computer means switching it on so that the operating system
loads and the desktop appears, ready for use.
Steps generally followed:
   1. Make sure the computer is plugged into a working power source (and, where used, that the surge
      protector/UPS is switched on).
   2. Press the power button on the system unit (and, on some setups, the power button on the monitor
      separately).
   3. Wait for the operating system to load fully - the screen will show a loading/starting screen and
      then the desktop.
   4. If required, enter a username and/or password to log in.

2. SHUTTING DOWN A COMPUTER, AND THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN "SHUT DOWN" AND "RESTART"
At Grade 7, pupils must be able to differentiate clearly between shutting down and restarting:
   - Shut down: this closes all open programs and files, saves system settings, and then switches the
     computer completely off so that no processes are running until it is switched on again.
   - Restart (reboot): this closes all open programs, then switches the computer off AND immediately
     switches it on again automatically, reloading the operating system from the beginning. Restarting
     is often used after installing new software, or when a computer is running slowly or behaving
     oddly, to "refresh" it.
It is important to always use the correct on-screen shut down/restart command (through the Start menu)
rather than simply switching off the power at the wall, because this can corrupt files or damage the
hard disk over time.

3. USE OF THE MOUSE - RIGHT-CLICKING
A mouse usually has (at least) a left button, a right button, and often a scroll wheel between them.
By Grade 7, pupils build on earlier grades (basic technique, then double-clicking) to focus on
RIGHT-CLICKING:
   - Left-click: used for the everyday tasks of selecting an item, opening it (with a double-click), or
     clicking a button/menu option.
   - Right-click: used to open a "shortcut menu" (also called a context menu) - a small list of options
     relevant to whatever was clicked on. For example, right-clicking on the desktop background usually
     shows options to change the background/display settings, arrange icons, or create a new folder;
     right-clicking on a file usually shows options such as copy, delete, rename, or print.
   - Scroll wheel: used to move up and down a page or list without using the scroll bar directly.

4. TASKS THAT REQUIRE RIGHT-CLICKING (Practical examples pupils should practise)
   - Right-clicking the desktop to open a shortcut menu for changing desktop display settings or
     arranging icons (for example, by name, by date, or by size, or turning "auto arrange" on).
   - Right-clicking a file or folder to see options like copy, cut, delete, or rename.
   - Right-clicking to access a "Refresh" option that updates what is shown on the screen.

5. GOOD PRACTICE WHEN USING A MOUSE
   - Hold the mouse gently, resting the palm and moving the whole hand rather than gripping it tightly.
   - Click precisely, without banging the buttons.
   - Keep the mouse on a clean, flat surface (or a mouse mat) so the pointer moves smoothly.

KEY TERMS
   - Boot/start up: the process of switching on a computer and loading the operating system.
   - Shut down: to completely switch off a computer after closing all programs safely.
   - Restart/reboot: to switch a computer off and then straight back on again automatically.
   - Right-click: pressing the right mouse button to open a shortcut (context) menu.
   - Shortcut menu / context menu: a small menu of options relevant to the item that was right-clicked.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Describe, in order, the steps for correctly starting up a computer.
   2. Explain the difference between "shut down" and "restart".
   3. Give two examples of tasks that need the mouse to be right-clicked rather than left-clicked.
   4. Why is it wrong to switch off a computer by pulling out the power plug while it is still running?
   5. What appears on the screen when you right-click on the desktop background?
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Desktop Features, Shortcut Menus, Screen Savers, and Date/Time/Volume Settings
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - BASIC SETTINGS AND FILE MANAGEMENT
TOPIC: Desktop Features and Settings (Start/Shortcut Menu, Screen Savers, Date, Time and Volume)

1. THE DESKTOP AND ITS FEATURES
The desktop is the main screen that appears after the computer has finished starting up. It works like
a virtual desk on which icons (small pictures representing programs, files or folders), the Start
button, and the Task bar are arranged.
Key desktop features Grade 7 pupils must know and use:
   - Icons: small pictures representing programs, files, folders or shortcuts; double-clicking an icon
     usually opens what it represents.
   - Start button/Start menu: normally at a corner of the screen, used to open installed programs,
     access settings, and shut down/restart the computer.
   - Task bar: a bar (often at the bottom of the screen) that shows the Start button, currently open
     programs/windows, and often the clock/date and volume icons, allowing quick switching between open
     programs.
   - Desktop background (wallpaper): the picture or colour displayed behind the icons.

2. USING THE START MENU AND SHORTCUT MENU FOR DESKTOP DISPLAYS
By Grade 7, pupils use BOTH the Start menu and the right-click shortcut menu to change how the desktop
looks, for example:
   - Changing the desktop background/wallpaper.
   - Arranging icons (by name, size, date, or turning on "auto arrange" so icons automatically line up
     neatly).
   - Adjusting screen resolution or display settings, where allowed by the teacher/system
     administrator.

3. SCREEN SAVERS
A screen saver is a moving picture or pattern that automatically appears on the screen after the
computer has been left idle (untouched) for a set period of time. Originally screen savers helped
prevent older types of screens from being permanently marked by a still image left on screen too long;
today they are mostly used for appearance, privacy (hiding the screen from view) and to indicate that a
computer has been idle. At Grade 7, pupils must be able to:
   - Select and apply a screen saver from the available options.
   - Change screen saver settings, including the "wait time" - the number of minutes of inactivity
     before the screen saver starts.

4. DATE, TIME AND VOLUME SETTINGS
   - Checking the current date and time, usually shown on the Task bar.
   - Changing date and time settings using a shortcut (for example, clicking directly on the clock
     display) rather than only through a longer menu path.
   - Adjusting the volume (sound level) using a shortcut, such as a volume icon on the Task bar, which
     is important for tasks like listening to an educational video, playing an audio file, or watching
     a presentation with sound.

5. WHY THESE SETTINGS MATTER
Being able to quickly and correctly adjust these everyday settings (rather than always calling a
teacher for help) is a basic digital literacy skill: knowing today's date can be needed when saving
schoolwork or filling in a form; volume control is needed for any task involving sound; screen savers
and desktop arrangement help keep a shared school computer looking tidy and working well for the next
user.

KEY TERMS
   - Desktop: the main screen shown after start-up, containing icons, the Start button and Task bar.
   - Icon: a small picture representing a program, file, folder or shortcut.
   - Task bar: the bar (usually at the bottom of the screen) showing the Start button, open programs,
     and system icons such as the clock and volume control.
   - Screen saver: a moving image that appears automatically after a period of inactivity.
   - Shortcut: a quick way of accessing a setting or command, often with fewer clicks than the full
     menu.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Name three features found on a typical computer desktop.
   2. What is the purpose of a screen saver?
   3. Describe how to change the wait time before a screen saver starts.
   4. Explain how to check and change the date and time using a shortcut.
   5. Give one reason why it is useful to be able to adjust the volume quickly using the Task bar.
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: My Computer, Drives, Files and Folders: Creating, Copying, Moving and Searching
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - BASIC SETTINGS AND FILE MANAGEMENT
TOPIC: My Computer, Drives, Files and Folders

1. WHAT IS "MY COMPUTER"?
"My Computer" (in some newer systems called "This PC") is an icon/window that lets the user see and
open all the storage drives connected to the computer, so files and folders can be found, organised,
copied or deleted.

2. DRIVES
A drive is a storage area that the computer gives a letter to, so it can be identified and opened.
Grade 7 pupils should recognise:
   - A drive: historically used for the floppy disk drive.
   - C drive: normally the computer's own internal hard disk, where the operating system, installed
     programs, and most saved files are usually stored by default.
   - D drive: often used for a CD/DVD drive, or sometimes a second storage partition/drive.
   - Removable drives: flash disks and external storage devices are usually given their own drive
     letter automatically when plugged in.
Pupils practise opening the A, C and D drives through "My Computer" and observing what is stored on
each.

3. FILES AND FOLDERS
   - A file is a single saved item, such as a document, picture, or spreadsheet, stored under a
     particular file name.
   - A folder (sometimes called a directory) is a container used to group and organise related files
     together, similar to a physical folder used to keep related paper documents together in a filing
     cabinet.
   - Folders can contain other folders (called sub-folders) as well as files, allowing information to
     be organised in a clear, tree-like structure - for example, a folder called "Grade 7" could contain
     sub-folders for each subject, and each subject sub-folder could contain the individual document
     files for that subject.

4. CREATING, COPYING AND MOVING FILES AND FOLDERS
   - Creating a folder: usually done by right-clicking in an empty space (inside a drive or another
     folder) and choosing "New" then "Folder", then typing a suitable name for it.
   - Copying: making a duplicate of a file/folder in another location while the original stays where it
     was. This is often done by right-clicking the file, choosing "Copy", opening the destination
     location, then right-clicking and choosing "Paste".
   - Moving: transferring a file/folder to a new location so it no longer remains in the original
     location. This can be done with "Cut" and "Paste" instead of "Copy" and "Paste", or by dragging the
     file/folder with the mouse to the new location.
   - It is important to choose sensible, clear names for folders and files, so that saved work can be
     found again easily later, for example naming a file "Grade7_Maths_Homework" rather than something
     unclear like "doc1".

5. SEARCHING FOR FILES AND FOLDERS
As files build up over time, it becomes harder to remember exactly where a particular file was saved.
Grade 7 pupils learn to search for files and folders:
   - By name: typing part or all of the file/folder name into a search box.
   - By date: searching using the date the file was created or last changed/saved, which is useful when
     the exact name has been forgotten but the pupil remembers roughly when the work was done.
   - By location: searching within a specific drive or folder, or across the whole computer.

6. WORKING WITH FILES AND FOLDERS ON DIFFERENT STORAGE DEVICES
Grade 7 pupils practise saving, copying, moving and deleting files and folders not only on the C drive
(hard disk), but also on other storage devices such as flash disks, CDs and DVDs, since schoolwork
often needs to be carried between the school computer laboratory and other computers (for example, an
internet café, a library, or a computer at home).

7. DELETING FILES AND FOLDERS
Deleting removes a file or folder from where it was stored. On the hard disk (C drive), a deleted file
usually goes first to the Recycle Bin (covered in the next topic) rather than disappearing immediately,
giving the user a chance to recover it if it was deleted by mistake. However, files deleted from other
storage devices such as flash disks are sometimes removed immediately and permanently, without passing
through a recycle bin - so pupils must be careful and sure before deleting files from a flash disk, CD
or DVD.

KEY TERMS
   - Drive: a labelled storage area/device recognised by the computer (for example, the C drive).
   - File: a single saved item of data, such as a document or picture.
   - Folder: a container used to organise and group related files together.
   - Copy: to duplicate a file/folder while keeping the original in place.
   - Move: to transfer a file/folder to a new location, removing it from the old one.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. What is the difference between a file and a folder?
   2. Describe how to create a new folder.
   3. Explain the difference between copying and moving a file.
   4. Describe two ways of searching for a file whose exact location has been forgotten.
   5. Why is it risky to delete a file from a flash disk compared to deleting one from the C drive?
   6. Suggest a sensible name for a spreadsheet file containing a Grade 7 class's end-of-term marks,
      and explain why good file naming matters.
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: The Recycle Bin and Printing Documents (Using Print Options)
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - BASIC SETTINGS AND FILE MANAGEMENT
TOPIC: The Recycle Bin; Printing Documents Using Options

1. THE RECYCLE BIN
The Recycle Bin is a special folder on the desktop that temporarily holds files and folders that have
been deleted from the hard disk (C drive). It works like a safety net: deleted items are not
immediately destroyed but are moved into the Recycle Bin first, and can be restored (put back) if they
were deleted by mistake.
   - Opening the Recycle Bin: double-clicking its icon shows everything currently inside it.
   - Displaying files/folders in the Recycle Bin: viewing what has been deleted, including the name and
     original location of each item.
   - Restoring files/folders: selecting an item inside the Recycle Bin and choosing "Restore" returns
     it to its original location, undoing the deletion.
   - Emptying the Recycle Bin: permanently deletes everything inside it, freeing up storage space but
     removing any chance of restoring those files afterwards. Because of this, pupils should always be
     certain before emptying the Recycle Bin.

2. PRINTING DOCUMENTS
Printing produces a paper (hard copy) version of a document, picture, spreadsheet or presentation
using a printer connected to the computer.

Ways of starting a print job:
   - Using a shortcut: for example, a keyboard shortcut, or clicking a print icon on the toolbar, which
     usually prints straight away using default settings.
   - Using the menu: opening the File menu and choosing "Print", which opens a dialogue box giving more
     control over how the document is printed.

3. USING PRINT OPTIONS (Grade 7 focus: page range and number of copies)
When printing through the menu/print dialogue box, the user can usually control:
   - Page range: choosing to print ALL pages of a document, or only specific pages/a range of pages
     (for example, "pages 2 to 4"), which saves paper and ink/toner when only part of a long document is
     needed.
   - Number of copies: choosing how many printed copies of the document are produced in one print job,
     instead of having to repeat the print command separately for each copy.
   - Choosing the correct printer, if more than one printer is available/connected.

4. WHY PRINT OPTIONS MATTER
Learning to set the page range and number of copies correctly avoids wasting paper, ink or toner -
resources that cost real money for a school - by preventing pupils from accidentally printing far more
pages or copies than are actually needed. It also saves time, since several copies of a document can be
produced from one print command rather than repeating "Print" over and over.

5. PREVIEWING BEFORE PRINTING
Where available, using "Print Preview" before actually printing lets the user see exactly how the
document will look on paper (margins, page breaks, layout) so mistakes can be corrected first, again
saving paper that would otherwise be wasted on an incorrectly formatted printout.

KEY TERMS
   - Recycle Bin: a temporary storage area for files deleted from the hard disk, from which they can be
     restored.
   - Restore: to return a deleted file or folder from the Recycle Bin to its original location.
   - Empty the Recycle Bin: to permanently delete everything held in the Recycle Bin.
   - Page range: the specific pages chosen to be printed, rather than the whole document.
   - Print Preview: a feature that shows how a document will appear once printed, before actually
     printing it.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. What is the purpose of the Recycle Bin?
   2. Explain the difference between deleting a file and emptying the Recycle Bin.
   3. Describe how to restore a file that was accidentally deleted.
   4. Explain two options that can be set when printing a document through the File menu.
   5. Why should a pupil use Print Preview before printing a long document?
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Word Processing: Loading the Program, the Screen Layout, and Keyboard Keys
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - WORD PROCESSING
TOPIC: Loading a Word Processing Program; the Word Processing Screen; Keyboard Keys and Their Uses

1. WHAT IS WORD PROCESSING?
Word processing is the use of a computer and special application software (a word processor) to type,
edit, format, save and print text documents such as letters, compositions, stories, reports and
notices, replacing much of the need to write documents entirely by hand.

2. LOADING (OPENING) A WORD PROCESSING PROGRAM
By Grade 7, pupils are expected to open a word processing program using BOTH methods:
   - Using the Start menu: clicking the Start button, then locating and selecting the word processing
     program from the list of installed programs.
   - Using an icon: double-clicking a word processor icon located on the desktop or Task bar.
Being able to use either method is useful because not every computer has a desktop icon set up, while
the Start menu will normally always list installed programs.

3. CLOSING (EXITING) A WORD PROCESSING PROGRAM
There are two common ways to close the program once finished:
   - Clicking the close icon (usually an "X" in the top corner of the window).
   - Using the "Close" command found inside the File menu.
Before closing, the user should always save any unsaved work, since closing without saving loses any
changes made since the last save.

4. THE WORD PROCESSING SCREEN
Grade 7 pupils build on earlier grades to understand the full working screen of a word processor:
   - Title bar: shows the name of the open document and the name of the program.
   - Menu bar: lists menu names (such as File, Edit, View, Insert, Format) that open drop-down lists
     of commands when clicked.
   - Toolbars: rows of small buttons/icons giving quick access to common commands (such as Bold, Print,
     Save) without having to open a full menu.
   - View on the menu bar: allows the user to change how the document is displayed on screen (for
     example, showing or hiding certain toolbars).
   - Scroll bars: bars (vertical and horizontal) at the edge of the window used to move up/down or
     left/right through a document that is bigger than the visible window.
   - Adding and removing toolbars: pupils practise choosing which toolbars are shown on screen, keeping
     only the most useful/most used ones visible to avoid a cluttered screen.

5. KEYBOARD KEYS AND THEIR USES (Grade 7 focus: frequently used keys, including function keys)
Building on earlier grades, Grade 7 pupils must identify and correctly use a wider range of keys:
   - Letter, number and symbol keys: used for ordinary typing.
   - Enter key: moves the cursor to a new line/paragraph, or confirms a command.
   - Backspace key: deletes the character immediately to the LEFT of the cursor.
   - Delete key: deletes the character immediately to the RIGHT of the cursor (or removes a selected/
     highlighted item).
   - Space bar: inserts a blank space.
   - Caps Lock key: switches typing between capital (upper case) and small (lower case) letters until
     switched off again.
   - Shift key: used together with another key to type a capital letter or the upper symbol on a key
     (held down while pressing the other key), and also used together with the arrow keys to select/
     highlight text.
   - Arrow keys: move the cursor up, down, left or right within a document, one step at a time.
   - Tab key: moves the cursor forward by a fixed distance (a "tab stop"), commonly used to indent the
     first line of a paragraph or to line up text/columns neatly.
   - Scroll Lock key: an older key, found on many keyboards, that in some programs changes what the
     arrow keys do (rather than moving the cursor, it can scroll the whole document instead); pupils are
     expected to be able to identify it, even though it is rarely used in modern word processors.
   - Insert key: on some keyboards, switches typing between "Insert mode" (new text is added without
     replacing existing text) and "Overtype mode" (new text types over/replaces existing text).
   - Function keys (F1 to F12, along the top of the keyboard): each is programmed to perform a
     specific shortcut action depending on the program being used (for example, F1 commonly opens
     "Help" in many programs).
   - Numeric keypad keys: the block of number keys, often on the right side of a full-size keyboard,
     useful for quickly typing numbers, such as when entering data into a spreadsheet.

6. TYPING SKILLS AT GRADE 7
Pupils are expected to move beyond typing single words or short sentences (done in earlier grades) to:
   - Typing using two hands, rather than one finger at a time, to build speed and accuracy.
   - Typing at an acceptable speed for their age and experience.
   - Typing full compositions, letters, and different kinds of text such as short reports, using
     correct punctuation and special characters (for example: ! ? , . ; " " ( ) % $ # @ * < >).
   - Playing age-appropriate typing/educational games as a fun way of practising keyboard familiarity
     and speed.

KEY TERMS
   - Word processor: application software used to create, edit, format and print text documents.
   - Toolbar: a row of icons/buttons giving quick access to commonly used commands.
   - Cursor: the blinking vertical line on screen showing where the next typed character will appear.
   - Function keys: the F1-F12 keys along the top of the keyboard, each performing a program-specific
     shortcut.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Describe two ways of opening (loading) a word processing program.
   2. Name three features found on the word processing screen (besides the typing area).
   3. Explain the difference between the Backspace key and the Delete key.
   4. What is the purpose of the Tab key in a word processing document?
   5. Explain what the Shift key can be used for, giving two different uses.
   6. Why is it important to learn to type using two hands rather than one finger?
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Word Processing: Selecting, Correcting and Editing Text (Cut, Copy, Paste, Find and Replace)
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - WORD PROCESSING
TOPIC: Selecting, Correcting and Editing Text

1. SELECTING (HIGHLIGHTING) TEXT
Before text can be formatted, deleted, copied or moved, it usually needs to be selected/highlighted
first, which shows the computer exactly which part of the document the next command should apply to.
By Grade 7, pupils select text using:
   - The mouse: clicking at the start of the text and dragging to the end while holding the mouse
     button down, or double-clicking a single word to select it, or triple-clicking to select a whole
     paragraph.
   - The keyboard: holding the Shift key and pressing the arrow keys to extend the selection character
     by character or line by line.
   - A combination of both mouse and keyboard, depending on which is quickest for the task at hand.

2. CHECKING AND CORRECTING SPELLING AND GRAMMAR
Most word processors automatically check spelling and, in many cases, grammar as the user types,
usually showing a coloured wavy underline beneath a suspected error.
   - Spell check: compares typed words against a built-in dictionary and flags words it does not
     recognise as possibly misspelt.
   - Grammar check: looks at how words are combined in sentences and flags likely grammar errors, such
     as subject-verb disagreement.
   - Pupils should understand an important limitation: the computer's dictionary is mainly built for
     standard English, so correctly spelt non-English words (such as Shona or Ndebele words used in a
     document) or specialised scientific/technical words may also be flagged as "errors" even though
     they are correct; the user (guided by the teacher) must use good judgement rather than blindly
     accepting every suggested correction.
   - Correcting errors is taught progressively - pupils are encouraged to notice and fix their own
     errors, not just rely completely on the computer.

3. FORMATTING RELATED TO TEXT SELECTION: ITALICS
Building on bold, underline, colour and alignment learnt in earlier grades, Grade 7 adds ITALICS -
slanted text used, for example, to emphasise a word, to show the title of a book, or for other stylistic
effect. Italics, like bold and underline, is applied by first selecting the text, then clicking the
Italic button/icon (or using its keyboard shortcut).

4. EDITING TEXT: CUTTING, COPYING AND PASTING
   - Copy and Paste: COPY makes a duplicate of the selected text, keeping the original text unchanged
     in its original place; PASTE then places that duplicated text at the new cursor position (in the
     same document or even in a different document).
   - Cut and Paste: CUT removes the selected text completely from its original place (storing it
     temporarily); PASTE then places it in the new position. This effectively MOVES text from one place
     to another, rather than duplicating it.
   - Both can be carried out using the Edit menu commands, or using toolbar icons, or using keyboard
     shortcuts; pupils are taught to first understand the Edit menu commands before being introduced to
     faster shortcuts, so that they understand what each action actually does.

5. CHANGING CASE
Word processors normally include a "change case" tool that can automatically convert selected text
between: UPPER CASE (all capital letters), lower case (all small letters), Title Case (First Letter Of
Each Word Capitalised), and Sentence case, without the user needing to retype the text by hand.

6. FIND AND REPLACE
   - Find: searches through the whole document for a specific word or phrase and highlights/jumps to
     each place it occurs, saving the time of reading through a long document manually.
   - Replace: works together with Find to automatically substitute a found word/phrase with a different
     one, either one at a time (with the user confirming each change) or throughout the whole document
     at once ("Replace All"). This is very useful, for example, if a pupil realises they have spelt a
     name incorrectly throughout an entire composition and needs to correct every occurrence quickly.

KEY TERMS
   - Select/highlight: to mark a portion of text so that a command will apply specifically to it.
   - Cut: to remove selected text/data, storing it temporarily so it can be placed elsewhere.
   - Copy: to duplicate selected text/data while leaving the original unchanged.
   - Paste: to insert previously cut or copied text/data at a new position.
   - Find and Replace: a tool used to search for a word/phrase in a document and substitute it with
     another.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Describe two ways of selecting text using the keyboard and mouse.
   2. Explain the difference between Cut-and-Paste and Copy-and-Paste.
   3. Why might the spell checker sometimes wrongly flag a correctly spelt word as an error?
   4. Describe how "Find and Replace" could be used to correct a name that was spelt wrongly many times
      in a long composition.
   5. Name the four common case options a "change case" tool usually offers.
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Word Processing: Formatting Documents (Fonts, Alignment, Line Spacing, Borders, Columns, Word Art, Margins, Page Numbering)
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - WORD PROCESSING
TOPIC: Formatting a Word Processing Document

1. WHAT IS FORMATTING?
Formatting means changing the appearance of text and of a whole document (rather than changing the
actual words), so that the document looks neat, professional, and easy to read, and to draw attention
to important parts.

2. CHARACTER-LEVEL FORMATTING
By Grade 7, pupils apply and combine the following formatting features learnt across earlier grades,
now with fuller control:
   - Bold: makes selected text thicker/darker, used to emphasise important words or headings.
   - Italics: slants selected text, also used for emphasis or for titles.
   - Underline: places a line beneath selected text.
   - Font type: the style/design of the lettering (for example, a plain, easy-to-read font versus a
     more decorative one); different fonts suit different purposes - a plain font for the main body of
     a letter, and perhaps a bolder or more decorative font for a heading.
   - Font size: how large or small the text appears, usually measured in "points"; headings are
     normally given a larger font size than the main body text.
   - Colour: changing the colour of text to highlight or decorate it, used sensibly so the document
     stays easy to read.

3. PARAGRAPH-LEVEL AND PAGE-LEVEL FORMATTING
   - Alignment: how text lines up on the page - Left alignment (the default, text starts evenly on the
     left), Right alignment (text ends evenly on the right), Centre alignment (text is centred between
     the margins, often used for headings/titles), and Justify (text is stretched so both the left and
     right edges line up evenly, commonly used in newspapers and books).
   - Line spacing: the amount of space between lines of text (for example, single spacing or double
     spacing); wider line spacing can make a document easier to read, or may be requested for a
     particular assignment format.
   - Borders: lines or decorative edges placed around a paragraph, a page, or a whole document, often
     used to make a certificate, poster or notice look neat and finished.
   - Columns: dividing text on a page into two or more vertical sections (like a newspaper layout),
     often used for newsletters or pamphlets.
   - Margins: the blank space left around the edges of a page (top, bottom, left and right), which keep
     text from running right to the very edge of the paper and leave room for binding or notes.
   - Page numbering: automatically adding and updating page numbers on each page of a multi-page
     document, so pages stay easy to keep in order when printed.

4. DECORATIVE FEATURES: WORD ART, AUTO SHAPES, SYMBOLS AND PICTURES
   - Word Art: a feature that turns typed text into a decorative graphic/picture-like heading, often
     used for titles of posters, certificates or projects, since it allows curved, coloured, shadowed or
     stylised text that plain formatting cannot achieve.
   - Auto Shapes: ready-made shapes (such as stars, arrows, circles, banners) that can be inserted,
     resized, coloured and combined to design patterns, diagrams or decorations within a document.
   - Inserting symbols and pictures: adding special characters not found directly on the keyboard (such
     as certain punctuation or mathematical symbols), or inserting pictures/clip art to illustrate a
     document.

5. TABULATION
Using the Tab key together with tab settings to line up text neatly into columns without using a full
table, useful for simple lists where items need to line up under each other precisely.

6. PUTTING IT ALL TOGETHER: DESIGNING A NEAT DOCUMENT
Grade 7 pupils are expected to combine several of the above features sensibly to design attractive,
readable documents such as compositions, letters, posters, or pamphlets - for example, using a larger,
bold, centred title in Word Art, body text in a plain readable font with justified alignment and
sensible line spacing, a border around the page, and page numbers if the document runs to more than one
page. Overusing too many colours, fonts or decorations at once, however, is discouraged, since it can
make a document look messy and harder to read rather than more professional.

KEY TERMS
   - Formatting: changing how a document looks (fonts, spacing, alignment, colour, borders, etc.)
     without changing the actual wording.
   - Alignment: how the edges of text line up on the page (left, right, centre, justify).
   - Margin: blank space left around the edges of a page.
   - Word Art: a feature that turns text into a decorative, picture-like design.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Explain the difference between "font type" and "font size".
   2. Name and describe all four types of text alignment.
   3. What is the purpose of margins on a page?
   4. Explain what Word Art is used for, and give one example of when it would be useful.
   5. Why might a document that uses too many different fonts and colours be considered poorly
      designed, even though each individual feature was used correctly?
   6. Describe how columns could be used to format a school newsletter.
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Word Processing: Saving, Opening and Storing Documents on Different Media
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - WORD PROCESSING
TOPIC: Saving, Opening and Closing Documents on the Hard Disk and Other Media

1. WHY SAVING IS IMPORTANT
Any document typed on a computer exists only in the computer's temporary working memory until it is
saved onto a storage device. If the computer loses power, freezes, or is closed without saving, unsaved
work is lost completely. Grade 7 pupils are therefore expected to understand saving thoroughly and to
save their work regularly while working, not only at the very end.

2. THE SAVE AND OPEN COMMANDS IN THE FILE MENU
   - Save: stores the current document to a chosen location under a chosen file name. The first time a
     new document is saved, the program asks for a file name and a location (this is sometimes called
     "Save As"); after that, clicking Save again simply updates the same file with the latest changes.
   - Save As: used to save a copy of a document under a NEW name or in a NEW location, while normally
     leaving the original saved file unchanged - useful, for example, for keeping an earlier draft
     safe while continuing to edit a new version separately.
   - Open: retrieves a previously saved document from storage so it can be viewed and edited again.
     This is normally done by browsing to the correct drive and folder, then double-clicking the
     required file, or by selecting it and choosing "Open".
   - Close: shuts the current document, prompting the user to save first if there are unsaved changes.
   - Exit: closes the whole word processing program, not just the current document.

3. SAVING AND OPENING ON DIFFERENT STORAGE MEDIA
Grade 7 pupils practise saving and opening documents not just on the C drive (hard disk), but also on
other media:
   - Compact disks (CDs): documents can be saved (written/"burnt") onto a CD, useful for keeping a
     backup copy or for handing work to someone else in a durable, widely-readable format.
   - Diskettes (floppy disks): recognised historically as an early portable storage option, though
     largely outdated today due to their very small storage capacity.
   - Flash disks: the most commonly used portable storage device today for moving documents between
     the school computer laboratory and other computers, since they are small, reusable, and hold a
     reasonably large amount of data.
Understanding how to save to and open from different media is a practical skill, since a Grade 7 pupil
may type a composition at school, save it on a flash disk, and then need to open and continue editing it
on a different computer at home, at a relative's house, or at an internet café.

4. GOOD FILE-SAVING HABITS
   - Choosing clear, descriptive file names (for example, "MyStory_John_Grade7" rather than
     "Document1"), so files are easy to identify later.
   - Saving work into a sensibly named folder (for example, a folder for the subject or the term),
     rather than leaving many files scattered loose on the desktop or directly in "My Documents".
   - Saving regularly while working on a long document, not only right at the end, in case of an
     unexpected power cut or computer freeze.
   - Keeping a backup copy of especially important documents on a second storage device.

KEY TERMS
   - Save: to store the current document to a chosen location and file name.
   - Save As: to save a copy of a document under a new name or in a new location.
   - Open: to retrieve a previously saved document from storage.
   - Storage media: physical devices used to store data, such as a hard disk, flash disk, or CD.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Explain the difference between "Save" and "Save As".
   2. Describe the steps for opening a document that was previously saved on a flash disk.
   3. Why is it good practice to save a long document several times while working on it, rather than
      only once at the very end?
   4. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of saving an important document onto only one storage
      device.
   5. Suggest a good, clear name for a Grade 7 pupil's saved composition about "My Weekend", and
      explain why it is a good choice.
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Spreadsheets: Introduction, Uses, Types and Structure
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - SPREADSHEETS
TOPIC: Introduction to a Spreadsheet - Definition, Uses, Types and Structure

1. WHAT IS A SPREADSHEET?
A spreadsheet is an application program (or the document created by such a program) used to organise,
calculate, analyse and present data - especially numbers - arranged neatly in rows and columns. A
spreadsheet automatically recalculates results whenever the underlying figures are changed, which is
far quicker and more reliable than reworking calculations by hand every time a number changes.

2. USES OF SPREADSHEETS
Grade 7 pupils must be able to state realistic uses of spreadsheets, such as:
   - Keeping and calculating school marks/results, including totals and averages for a class.
   - Managing household or personal budgets - listing income and expenses and calculating balances.
   - Keeping simple business records, such as sales, stock levels, and profit calculations for a small
     family business, a common and very relevant example in the Zimbabwean context.
   - Producing charts and graphs from data, to present information visually (for example, showing rainfall
     figures for different months, or comparing crop yields).
   - Doing quick "what if" calculations - for example, seeing how a total changes automatically if one
     figure in the list is changed.

3. TYPES OF SPREADSHEETS
   - Manual spreadsheets: traditional paper-based ledgers/tables where rows and columns of figures are
     written and calculated by hand, used long before computers, and still used today in some small,
     informal settings.
   - Computerised spreadsheets: spreadsheets created and calculated using spreadsheet software on a
     computer, which automatically perform calculations, are far quicker to update, and can easily be
     copied, saved, printed, or turned into charts.
Pupils should be able to explain that computerised spreadsheets have largely replaced manual ones for
serious or repeated calculations, because they save time and reduce human calculation errors, while
still understanding that the underlying idea (organising figures into rows and columns) is the same in
both.

4. THE STRUCTURE OF A COMPUTERISED SPREADSHEET
Grade 7 pupils must know and correctly identify each of the following structural parts:
   - Workbook: the entire spreadsheet file, which can contain one or more worksheets.
   - Worksheet (sheet): a single "page" or grid within a workbook, made up of rows and columns; a
     workbook can have several worksheets, accessible using sheet tabs.
   - Sheet tabs: small labelled tabs (often at the bottom of the screen) used to switch between
     different worksheets within the same workbook.
   - Rows: horizontal lines of cells running left to right, normally labelled with numbers (1, 2, 3, ...).
   - Columns: vertical lines of cells running top to bottom, normally labelled with letters (A, B, C, ...).
   - Row headings and column headings: the numbers and letters used to label rows and columns.
   - Cell: the small box formed where a row and a column meet; this is where individual pieces of data
     (a number, a word, or a formula) are entered.
   - Cell name (cell reference): the label identifying a specific cell, formed by combining its column
     letter and row number (for example, cell B3 is where column B meets row 3).
   - Cell pointer: the highlighted box/outline showing which cell is currently selected/active and
