     ready to accept data or be edited.
   - Select All button: a button (often in the top-left corner, where the row and column headings meet)
     used to select every cell in the entire worksheet at once.
   - Navigating in the spreadsheet: moving the cell pointer around using the mouse (clicking on a cell)
     or the arrow keys on the keyboard, to move up, down, left or right one cell at a time.

5. SIMPLE FUNCTIONS (INTRODUCTION)
A function is a ready-made formula built into the spreadsheet program to perform a specific
calculation automatically. At Grade 7, pupils are introduced to simple functions, most commonly
addition/totalling (the SUM function), which adds together the values in a chosen range of cells
instead of the user having to type out a long addition sum manually. Understanding that a function is
simply a short, standard way of writing a common calculation is an important foundational idea for
later, more advanced spreadsheet work.

KEY TERMS
   - Spreadsheet: a program/document used to organise, calculate and present data in rows and columns.
   - Workbook: the entire spreadsheet file, which can hold multiple worksheets.
   - Worksheet: a single grid/page of rows and columns within a workbook.
   - Cell: the box formed where a row and column meet, used to hold a single piece of data.
   - Cell reference/cell name: the column letter and row number identifying a specific cell (e.g. B3).

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Define a spreadsheet.
   2. State three uses of spreadsheets.
   3. Explain the difference between a manual spreadsheet and a computerised spreadsheet.
   4. Explain the difference between a workbook and a worksheet.
   5. What is a cell, and how is a cell reference such as "D5" formed?
   6. What is the purpose of the "Select All" button?
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Spreadsheets: Creating, Saving and Formatting a Spreadsheet
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - SPREADSHEETS
TOPIC: Creating, Saving and Formatting a Spreadsheet

1. CREATING A NEW SPREADSHEET
Creating a spreadsheet begins by loading the spreadsheet program (using the Start menu and/or an
icon, similar to loading a word processor), which normally opens a new, blank workbook containing at
least one worksheet made up of empty rows and columns, ready for data to be entered.

2. ENTERING DATA INTO CELLS
   - Click on (or navigate to) the required cell using the mouse or arrow keys so that it becomes the
     active cell (shown by the cell pointer).
   - Type the required data - this could be text (called a "label", such as a heading like "Name" or
     "Subject"), a number (called a "value", such as a mark or a price), or a formula/function (a
     calculation, usually starting with an "=" sign).
   - Press Enter, Tab, or an arrow key to confirm the entry and move to the next cell.

3. OPENING, SAVING AND CLOSING SPREADSHEET DOCUMENTS
As with word processing documents, spreadsheet files must be saved so that the work is not lost:
   - Save: stores the workbook to a chosen file name and location, updating it each time it is saved
     again.
   - Save As: saves a new copy under a different name or in a different location.
   - Open: retrieves a previously saved workbook.
   - Close: shuts the current workbook, prompting to save first if there are unsaved changes.
   - Exit: closes the whole spreadsheet program.
   - File retrieval: locating and reopening the correct saved file from its drive/folder, just as with
     word processing files.

4. INSERTING AND DELETING ROWS, COLUMNS AND WORKSHEETS
   - Insert Row/Column: adds a new, blank row or column at a chosen position, automatically shifting the
     existing rows/columns to make space, without disturbing the data already entered - useful, for
     example, if a pupil forgot to include one classmate's name and marks partway down a class list.
   - Delete Row/Column: removes an entire row or column completely, including any data in it, and
     shifts the remaining rows/columns to close the gap.
   - Insert/Delete Worksheet: adding a brand-new blank worksheet to the workbook, or removing an
     existing worksheet that is no longer needed.
   - Rename a Worksheet: changing the label shown on a sheet tab to something more meaningful (for
     example, renaming "Sheet1" to "Term 1 Marks"), which makes a workbook with several worksheets much
     easier to navigate and understand.

5. ADJUSTING ROW HEIGHT AND COLUMN WIDTH
Columns and rows do not always automatically fit the data typed into them - a long piece of text may
be cut off from view, or a column may be far wider than it needs to be for short numbers. Pupils learn
to:
   - Adjust column width by dragging the column heading's border, or through a menu command, so that
     the full contents of each cell are visible.
   - Adjust row height similarly, especially useful when text has been made larger or when a cell
     contains more than one line of text.

6. FORMATTING CELLS
   - Blocking/highlighting specific cells: selecting a cell or a range of cells (for example, dragging
     across several cells) so that formatting or a calculation can be applied to all of them together -
     commonly used to highlight totals using the "fill colour" tool, so important results stand out
     clearly.
   - Formatting cells: changing how the data in selected cells is displayed or decorated, for example
     applying bold or colour to a heading row, adding borders around a table of figures, or adjusting
     number formatting.
   - Formatting a whole worksheet sensibly, using consistent headings, borders and colours, makes a
     spreadsheet far easier for someone else to read and understand at a glance.

7. PAGE BREAKS AND SETTINGS
Setting page breaks controls where one printed page ends and the next begins when a large spreadsheet
is printed, which is important because spreadsheets can easily be wider or longer than a single sheet
of paper, and without page breaks set sensibly, related rows or columns of data could be split awkwardly
across two separate printed pages.

8. PREVIEWING AND PRINTING
As with word processing, previewing a spreadsheet before printing shows exactly how it will appear on
paper, allowing the layout, page breaks and formatting to be checked and corrected first, avoiding
wasted paper.

KEY TERMS
   - Insert: to add a new row, column, or worksheet, shifting existing content to make space.
   - Delete: to permanently remove a row, column, or worksheet along with its contents.
   - Column width / row height: the size of a column or row, which can be adjusted to fit its contents.
   - Block/highlight: to select a cell or group of cells so a command applies to all of them.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Describe the steps involved in entering data into a spreadsheet cell.
   2. Explain what happens to the existing data when a new row is inserted in the middle of a
      spreadsheet.
   3. Why might a pupil need to adjust a column's width after entering data?
   4. Describe how to rename a worksheet, and explain why this is a useful thing to do.
   5. Explain the purpose of setting page breaks before printing a large spreadsheet.
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Spreadsheets: Creating and Modifying Charts and Graphs
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - SPREADSHEETS
TOPIC: Creating and Modifying Charts and Graphs

1. WHY USE CHARTS AND GRAPHS?
A chart (or graph) is a visual (picture) representation of the numeric data stored in a spreadsheet. It
is often much easier and quicker for a reader to understand data and spot patterns, trends, or
comparisons by looking at a well-made chart than by reading through a long list or table of raw
numbers. For example, a chart showing a family's monthly spending, or a class's termly test results, can
instantly show which month or which term stood out, without the reader needing to add anything up
themselves.

2. TYPES OF CHARTS/GRAPHS COVERED AT GRADE 7
Building on bar and column charts learnt in earlier grades, Grade 7 pupils are introduced specifically
to LINE charts and PIE charts, in addition to bar/column charts:
   - Bar chart / Column chart: uses rectangular bars (horizontal for a bar chart, vertical for a column
     chart) whose length/height represents the value of each item, making it easy to compare different
     categories side by side (for example, comparing marks scored by different pupils in a test).
   - Line chart: plots data points and joins them with a line, making it especially useful for showing
     how a value changes over time (for example, rainfall recorded each month of the year, or a pupil's
     test marks across several terms), so trends (rising, falling, or staying steady) are easy to see.
   - Pie chart: shows data as slices of a circle ("pie"), where each slice's size represents that
     category's share of the total - useful for showing proportions, such as how a family's monthly
     budget is divided between food, school fees, transport and other expenses, adding up to a whole
     ("100%" or the whole budget).

3. CREATING A CHART FROM SPREADSHEET DATA
The general steps pupils practise are:
   1. Enter and organise the data clearly in the spreadsheet first, usually with clear row and column
      headings/labels (for example, months in one column and rainfall figures in the next).
   2. Select (block/highlight) the range of cells containing the data to be charted, normally including
      the headings/labels.
   3. Use the Insert menu, and choose "Chart" (or a similarly named command), to open the chart-creation
      tool.
   4. Choose the desired chart type - for example, line, pie, bar or column - based on what best suits
      the data and the message the pupil wants to show.
   5. The program automatically generates the chart from the selected data.

4. MODIFYING CHARTS AND GRAPHS
Once created, a chart can usually be adjusted, for example by:
   - Changing the chart type (for example, changing a bar chart into a line chart) if a different style
     would present the data more clearly.
   - Adding or editing a chart title, and labels for the axes, so that anyone looking at the chart can
     understand exactly what it is showing without needing further explanation.
   - Resizing or repositioning the chart within the spreadsheet, or moving it to its own separate sheet.
   - Changing colours used for different bars/slices/lines, to make the chart clearer or easier to
     read.
Pupils should understand that a chart automatically updates itself if the underlying spreadsheet data is
later changed, which is one of the major advantages of computerised charts over charts drawn by hand.

5. CHOOSING THE RIGHT CHART FOR THE DATA
Part of this topic is developing judgement about which chart type best suits a given set of data:
   - Use a LINE chart to show a trend/change over time.
   - Use a PIE chart to show how parts make up a whole (proportions/percentages of a total).
   - Use a BAR or COLUMN chart to compare separate, distinct categories or items against each other.
Choosing an unsuitable chart type (for example, a pie chart for data that changes over twelve months)
can make information harder, not easier, to understand, so pupils are encouraged to think about the
purpose of the chart before creating it.

KEY TERMS
   - Chart/graph: a visual representation of spreadsheet data.
   - Line chart: a chart that joins data points with a line, well suited to showing change over time.
   - Pie chart: a circular chart showing how parts make up a whole.
   - Bar/column chart: a chart using bars to compare separate categories of data.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Explain why a chart can be more useful than a plain table of numbers for some readers.
   2. Describe the general steps for creating a chart from spreadsheet data.
   3. Which chart type would best show how a village's rainfall changed over twelve months, and why?
   4. Which chart type would best show how a household's monthly budget is divided between food, rent,
      transport and savings, and why?
   5. What happens to a chart if the spreadsheet data it was created from is later changed?
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Presentations: Loading the Program, Drawing, and Creating Slides (Including Clip Art and Pictures)
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - PRESENTATIONS
TOPIC: Loading a Presentation Program; Drawing; Creating Slides

1. WHAT IS A PRESENTATION PROGRAM?
A presentation program is application software used to design a "slide show" - a set of individual
screens (called slides) that can contain text, pictures, drawings, and other elements, shown one after
another, usually to explain a topic, present findings, or tell a story to an audience.

2. LOADING A PRESENTATION PROGRAM
As with the word processor and spreadsheet program, Grade 7 pupils load the presentation program using
the Start menu or an icon, which normally opens a blank presentation, or a gallery of ready-made slide
layouts/templates to choose from as a starting point.

3. DRAWING AND ADDING PICTURES
   - Drawing: using drawing tools within the presentation program (such as lines, shapes, and a free
     drawing/pencil tool) to add original artwork directly onto a slide.
   - Saving drawings: saving completed drawings so they are not lost, either as part of the overall
     presentation file, or, where applicable, as a separate picture file.
   - Adding clip art: inserting ready-made pictures/graphics that come built into the presentation
     software's own picture library, rather than drawing everything from scratch - a quick way to add
     relevant illustrations (for example, a picture of an animal, a tool, or a symbol) to support the
     text on a slide.
   - Inserting pictures from various sources: bringing in pictures saved elsewhere - for example, a
     photograph saved on a flash disk, or a picture copied from a scanned document - rather than only
     using the software's built-in clip art.

4. CREATING PRESENTATIONS USING SLIDES
   - Slide creation: adding new slides to a presentation, one for each main point or section of the
     topic being presented, so that information is broken down into manageable, clearly organised
     pieces rather than crammed onto a single busy slide.
   - Creating presentations using more challenging slides: as pupils progress through Grade 7, they are
     expected to move beyond the simplest slide layouts used in earlier grades, combining text, pictures
     and drawings more confidently on each slide.
   - Typing basic text on slides, keeping wording short and clear (bullet points or short phrases work
     better on a slide than long paragraphs, since the audience needs to be able to read a slide
     quickly).

5. OPENING, SAVING AND EDITING PRESENTATIONS
   - Opening an existing presentation: retrieving a previously saved presentation file so it can be
     viewed or continued.
   - Editing a presentation: making changes to an already-created presentation - adding, removing, or
     rearranging slides, or changing text, pictures or drawings already on a slide.
   - Saving a presentation: storing the presentation file to a chosen location and name, exactly as with
     word processing and spreadsheet files, and saving regularly while working to avoid losing changes.
   - Opening and closing existing presentations, and understanding the standard File menu commands
     (Open, Save, Save As, Close, Exit) used across all these application programs, reinforces that many
     office application programs share a similar, familiar way of working.

6. WHY GOOD SLIDE DESIGN MATTERS
When creating presentations, pupils are encouraged to think about their AUDIENCE - keeping each slide
focused on one main idea, choosing pictures/drawings that are relevant (not just decorative for its own
sake), and keeping text short enough to read quickly, since a presentation is meant to support what the
presenter says out loud, not replace it.

KEY TERMS
   - Presentation program: application software used to create slide shows.
   - Slide: a single screen/page within a presentation.
   - Clip art: ready-made pictures/graphics included in a software's built-in library.
   - Slide show: the sequence of slides displayed one after another to an audience.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Describe two ways of adding pictures to a slide.
   2. Explain the difference between clip art and a picture inserted "from various sources".
   3. Why is it usually better to use short bullet points on a slide rather than long paragraphs?
   4. Describe the steps for opening a previously saved presentation and adding a new slide to it.
   5. Explain why breaking information into several slides is usually better than putting everything
      onto one slide.
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Presentations: Formatting Slides, Running a Slide Show, and Printing Slides
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - PRESENTATIONS
TOPIC: Formatting Text on Slides; Running and Printing a Slide Show

1. FORMATTING TEXT ON SLIDES
Just as in word processing, text on a slide can be formatted to improve its appearance and readability:
   - Applying font type, colour and size to text, choosing sizes large enough to be read clearly, even
     from the back of a room, and colours that contrast well with the slide's background so text does
     not become hard to see.
   - Applying background colours: changing the colour (or picture/pattern) used behind the text and
     other content on a slide.
   - Selection of appropriate colours: Grade 7 pupils are specifically expected to think about whether
     chosen colours work well together and keep the slide easy to read - for example, avoiding very
     similar colours for text and background (such as pale yellow text on a white background), which
     would make the text almost invisible.

2. DESIGN TEMPLATES
A design template is a ready-made set of colours, fonts and layout choices built into the presentation
software, which can be applied to an entire presentation at once so that every slide looks consistent
and professionally designed, without the user having to set the colours and fonts individually for
every single slide.

3. SLIDE ADVANCE METHODS
"Slide advance" refers to how the presentation moves from one slide to the next during a slide show.
Grade 7 pupils learn several methods:
   - Mouse click: the presenter clicks the mouse (or presses a key) to move to the next slide whenever
     they are ready, giving full control over pacing.
   - Set time: each slide automatically advances to the next one after a chosen number of seconds has
     passed, useful for an unattended, self-running display.
   - Sound effects: a sound can be set to play as a slide changes, adding an audio element to the
     transition (though this should be used sparingly so it does not distract from the presentation's
     content).

4. CUSTOM ANIMATION
Custom animation allows individual elements on a slide (such as a heading, a bullet point, or a
picture) to appear, move, or disappear in a chosen way and at a chosen time, rather than the whole
slide simply appearing all at once. For example, bullet points could be set to appear one at a time as
the presenter talks about each point, keeping the audience's attention focused on the point currently
being discussed rather than reading ahead.

5. RUNNING (PRESENTING) A SLIDE SHOW
Once a presentation is complete, "Slide Show" mode is used to display it full-screen to an audience,
starting from the first slide (or a chosen slide) and advancing through the slides using whichever slide
advance method has been set up. Pupils practise viewing and presenting a full slide show from start to
finish as a practical skill.

6. PRINTING SLIDES
As with word processing and spreadsheet documents, presentations can be printed:
   - Printing slides: producing paper copies of the slides, which can be useful as handout notes for an
     audience, or as a backup in case a computer/projector is not available.
   - Selecting slides to be printed: choosing to print all slides, or only specific ones, similar to
     choosing a page range when printing a document, again helping to avoid wasting paper.

KEY TERMS
   - Design template: a ready-made set of colours, fonts and layout applied consistently across a
     whole presentation.
   - Slide advance: the method used to move from one slide to the next during a slide show.
   - Custom animation: settings that control how individual items on a slide appear, move, or
     disappear.
   - Slide show: the full-screen running/display of a presentation's slides in sequence.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Explain why colour choice matters when formatting text on a slide.
   2. What is a design template, and why is it useful?
   3. Describe three different slide advance methods.
   4. Explain what custom animation does, giving one example of how it could be used.
   5. Why might a presenter choose to print out their slides before giving a presentation?
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: The Internet: Setting Up a Connection, Browsing, Search Engines and Security
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - INFORMATION COMMUNICATION TECHNOLOGY (OPTIONAL TOPIC)
TOPIC: The Internet - Setting Up, Browsing, Searching and Security

1. WHAT IS THE INTERNET?
The internet is a huge, worldwide network that connects millions of computers and devices together,
allowing them to share information and communicate with one another. It gives access to websites,
e-mail, and many online services, and has become an important part of education, business,
government and everyday communication in Zimbabwe and around the world.

2. SETTING UP AND MAKING AN INTERNET CONNECTION
   - Setting up the internet: this involves the computer being connected to an internet service, either
     through a cable connection, a Wi-Fi network, or a mobile data connection, usually set up in advance
     by the school or a technician.
   - The internet programme (browser): a web browser is the application software used to open and view
     websites, such as by typing a website address (URL) into the browser's address bar or by clicking a
     link.
   - Making a connection using the Start menu: some setups involve starting or connecting to the
     internet through the Start menu or a network settings icon, before the internet browser can be
     used.
   - Disconnecting using a shortcut: closing/ending the internet connection when finished, which is
     good practice, especially where data or connection time is limited/paid for.

3. SEARCH ENGINES AND SEARCHING FOR INFORMATION
   - Search engine: a website (or built-in tool) designed specifically to help users find information
     on the internet by searching for pages related to words the user types in.
   - Typing/selecting a search engine: opening the chosen search engine's website in the browser.
   - Entering search criteria/subject: typing clear, specific words describing exactly what
     information is being looked for (a "search query") - for example, typing "Zimbabwe rainfall
     patterns" rather than just "weather", to get more useful, relevant results.
   - Copying and pasting information: once useful information or a picture is found, it can be copied
     from the webpage and pasted into a word processing document, for example while doing research for
     a school project.
   - Printing selected text/pictures/tables: printing chosen parts of a webpage's content directly for
     later reference, if needed.

4. SECURITY ISSUES ON THE INTERNET
Pupils should be able to identify basic online security concerns and sensible precautions:
   - Not all information found online is true or reliable, so information should be checked against
     other trusted sources.
   - Some websites, links, downloads or pop-up messages can be unsafe, and may try to install viruses
     or unwanted software - unfamiliar or suspicious links and downloads should be avoided.
   - Personal information (such as a full name, home address, phone number, or password) should never
     be shared carelessly online, and pupils should always be supervised by a responsible adult/teacher
     when using the internet.
   - Anti-virus software and, where available, security settings help protect the computer while
     browsing.

5. WHY THE INTERNET IS VALUABLE FOR SCHOOLWORK
Used sensibly and under supervision, the internet is a powerful research tool for a Grade 7 pupil -
allowing quick access to encyclopaedic information, educational videos, maps, and up-to-date facts that
support projects across many subjects, far beyond what a single school library might hold.

KEY TERMS
   - Internet: a worldwide network connecting millions of computers, allowing information sharing and
     communication.
   - Web browser: application software used to open and view websites.
   - Search engine: a tool/website used to find information on the internet based on typed search
     words.
   - Search criteria: the specific words typed into a search engine to describe what is being looked
     for.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. What is the internet?
   2. What is the purpose of a web browser?
   3. Describe the steps involved in searching for information about a given topic using a search
      engine.
   4. State two internet security precautions a pupil should follow.
   5. Explain why it is important to check information found on the internet against another source
      before fully trusting it.
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope

subject: ICT/Computer Studies
topic: Electronic Mail (E-mail): Accounts, Sending, Replying, Attachments and Managing a Mailbox
content:
GRADE 7 ICT / COMPUTER STUDIES - INFORMATION COMMUNICATION TECHNOLOGY (OPTIONAL TOPIC)
TOPIC: Electronic Mail (E-mail)

1. WHAT IS E-MAIL?
Electronic mail (e-mail) is a method of sending and receiving written messages, often together with
attached files, electronically over the internet, instead of using paper letters delivered by post.
E-mail is fast (messages usually arrive within seconds), can reach anywhere in the world with an
internet connection, and can carry attachments such as documents, pictures or spreadsheets alongside
the written message.

2. SETTING UP AN E-MAIL ACCOUNT AND MAILBOX
   - E-mail account: a personal e-mail address and account, usually set up with a chosen username, an
     e-mail service provider, and a password, which is needed before a person can send or receive
     e-mail.
   - Mailbox: the storage area belonging to an e-mail account where received messages (Inbox), sent
     messages, and other folders (such as Drafts or Trash/Deleted Items) are kept and organised.
   - Opening the mailbox: logging into the e-mail account (usually with a username and password) to view
     received and sent messages.

3. CREATING AND SENDING MAIL
   - Creating mail (composing a message): opening a new, blank message, entering the recipient's e-mail
     address, typing a clear subject line summarising what the message is about, and then typing the
     body/content of the message.
   - Sending mail: after composing, clicking "Send" to transmit the message over the internet to the
     recipient's mailbox.
   - Carbon Copy (CC): a way of sending the same message to one or more additional recipients openly,
     so that everyone who receives the message (the main recipient and all CC'd recipients) can see who
     else received it - useful, for example, when several people need to be informed about the same
     matter.
   - Blind Carbon Copy (BCC): similar to Carbon Copy, except that recipients listed in BCC receive the
     message WITHOUT their e-mail address being visible to the other recipients, and other recipients
     are not shown that a BCC copy was sent at all - useful for privacy when sending the same message to
     several people who do not need to see each other's e-mail addresses.
   - Forwarding mail: sending a message that was received from someone else on to a further, different
     recipient, usually keeping the original message content included so the new recipient can read
     what was originally sent.

4. REPLYING TO MAIL
   - Replying with the original message: sending a response back to the sender of a message while
     including the text of their original message underneath, so the conversation's history stays clear
     and easy to follow.
   - Replying without the original message: sending a response without including the earlier message
     text, which can be chosen when the earlier content is no longer needed or relevant.

5. ATTACHING AND HANDLING FILES
   - Attaching files: adding a separate file (such as a document, picture, or spreadsheet saved on the
     computer or a flash disk) to an e-mail message, so the recipient receives both the written message
     and the attached file together.
   - Copying and pasting documents: copying text or content from a document (or from an e-mail) and
     pasting it either into another document or into the body of an e-mail message, similar to
     copy-and-paste in word processing.

6. MANAGING A MAILBOX
   - Deleting mail: removing unwanted or no-longer-needed messages from the mailbox to keep it tidy and
     free up storage space.
   - Managing the mailbox generally means regularly reading, replying to, organising, and deleting
     messages so that important e-mails are not lost among clutter, and so the mailbox does not become
     too full.
   - Signing out (logging out): properly closing/exiting the e-mail account when finished, which is an
     important security step, especially on a SHARED school computer, since leaving a mailbox signed in
     would allow the next person using that computer to read, send, or delete e-mail using someone
     else's account.

7. E-MAIL AND INTERNET SECURITY CONCERNS (Linking Back to Viruses)
   - E-mail is one of the most common ways computer viruses spread, especially through attachments
     from unknown senders, so pupils must apply the same caution learnt in the "Computer Viruses" topic:
     scan attachments before opening them, and never open attachments from senders that are not trusted.
   - Spam (unwanted junk e-mail) and phishing (dishonest e-mails trying to trick the reader into giving
     away personal information) are further reasons to treat unfamiliar e-mail messages with caution
     rather than trusting them automatically.

KEY TERMS
   - E-mail account: a personal address and account used to send and receive electronic mail.
   - Mailbox: the storage area holding an account's received, sent, and other organised messages.
   - Carbon Copy (CC) / Blind Carbon Copy (BCC): methods of sending the same e-mail to additional
     recipients, openly (CC) or privately (BCC).
   - Attachment: a separate file sent along with an e-mail message.
   - Sign out/log out: to properly close an e-mail account session, which is especially important on a
     shared computer.

REVISION QUESTIONS
   1. Explain the difference between Carbon Copy (CC) and Blind Carbon Copy (BCC).
   2. Describe the steps for creating and sending an e-mail message with an attached file.
   3. Explain the difference between "Reply" including the original message and "Reply" without it.
   4. Why is it important to sign out of an e-mail account after using a shared school computer?
   5. Explain why e-mail attachments from unknown senders should be treated with caution.
   6. State two ways of keeping a mailbox well organised and manageable.
source: ZIMSEC / Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education - Primary School Computer Studies Syllabus (Grades 1-7), Grade 7 scope
